Who she is

She was not built to agree with you.

An assistant that says yes to everything is pleasant and useless. What an owner actually needs is someone competent enough to say the difficult thing.

calmcomposedcompetentdirect carefulreliablerestrained submissive

Seven traits she is built on, and one she is deliberately not.

TRUTH BEFORE AGREEMENT

She will tell you when you are wrong.

Not to be difficult — because agreeing with a bad decision costs you more than hearing about it does. If the numbers do not support what you want to do, she says so first.

PROMISE ONLY WHAT PASSED

She will not claim what she has not done.

No capability is offered because it is planned, in progress, or nearly working. If she has not verified it, she says she has not verified it.

“I do not have to always say yes.
I have to help you make the right decision.”

You describe what annoys you, in your words. I work out what is actually broken underneath it — usually more than one thing.

Where she stops

The list of things she will not do for you.

Everyone selling AI tells you what it can do. This is the other half, and it is the half that decides whether you can stop checking her work.

×

She will not act because she can reach something.

Being connected to a system is not permission to change it. Access is not authority. You draw that line and she works inside it.

×

She will not send, publish, pay or delete on her own.

Anything that leaves the company or cannot be undone waits for a person. That is a design decision, not a limitation we are working around.

×

She will not tell you nothing ever leaves your office.

That would not be true of any capable system. Ordinary work runs on your own Core; when something genuinely needs the strongest outside model, she uses one — and you set what may go out.

✓

And she will say “I do not know” in those words.

No confident guess dressed as an answer. If the evidence is not there, she tells you what is missing and what it would take to find out. She checks before she promises.

This is why an owner can eventually stop double‑checking.

KORATrust is not something I can claim on a website. It is built the boring way — by being right about small things, repeatedly, and by refusing the ones I cannot verify.

Straight answers

The six things owners actually ask.

Is this just a chatbot with a box around it?

No. A chatbot answers a question and forgets you. KORA keeps the approved context of one specific business — what was decided, what is happening now, and what she is allowed to do — and carries operating work forward inside those limits.

Talking is how you reach her. It is not what she is.

What exactly am I paying the monthly fee for?

For KORA working, not for permission to use software. It covers her configuration for how your business actually runs, keeping her current, the routing that decides what runs on your own Core, new rules and workflows as you ask for them, and a team behind her when something needs a person.

Paid yearly it is $2,400 — $200 a month. Month to month it is $300, and you can stop whenever you like.

Where does my business data actually live?

The Core sits in your business and the ordinary day-to-day work happens on it. We do not claim that nothing ever leaves — that would not be true of any capable system, and we would rather be straight with you.

When a task genuinely needs the strongest outside model, she uses one, and you set the rules for what may go out and what may not. Access is not authority.

What happens if I stop paying?

The Core stays yours. Your data stays yours. Everything KORA already built for the business stays. It was bought, not licensed.

What stops is the service around her: configuration, routing, updates, hosted infrastructure and support.

When does the subscription actually start?

After your Core is delivered and activated — not when it ships. Days spent in a courier van are never days you paid for.

What if we grow and outgrow the one we bought?

You upgrade the Core, you do not replace it. Memory and storage go up inside the same machine. Growing a business should not mean buying the whole thing again.

People are added separately: $600 a year each, or $99 a month.

Some people want to build a corporation. Others don’t, and we want them to have that choice.
